blocks.text: Neck examination is an essential component of the general physical examination. It assesses the lymph nodes, thyroid gland, trachea, major blood vessels, salivary glands, cervical spine, and other neck structures. It may reveal diseases involving the thyroid, lymphatic system, respiratory tract, cardiovascular system, and head and neck.
The goal in an OSCE is to demonstrate a systematic examination, identify abnormalities, interpret your findings, and present them clearly to the examiner.
Before examining the neck, identify these important landmarks.

rows: Approximately at C3; lies above the thyroid cartilage
Forms the laryngeal prominence, commonly called the Adam's apple
Firm ring below the thyroid cartilage, around C6
Lies anteriorly over the upper trachea, with two lobes joined by an isthmus
Midline airway below the cricoid cartilage
Prominent muscle running from the mastoid process to the sternum and clavicle
Run deep to the SCM on either side of the neck
Distributed around the jaw, ears, neck, and supraclavicular fossae

blocks.text: Important OSCE principle: Examine the neck systematically, comparing both sides and proceeding from general inspection to palpation and relevant special tests.

items: Measuring tape or ruler, if required

blocks.text: Tongue depressor and pen torch if examining the oral cavity for a related lesion
Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity.
Explain the examination and obtain consent.
Ask whether the patient has neck pain or tenderness before palpation.
Position the patient sitting upright, with the neck exposed from the chin to the upper chest and shoulders appropriately covered.
Stand in front of the patient for inspection and most anterior examinations.
Sit or stand behind the patient when palpating the thyroid gland and posterior cervical structures.
Ask the patient to relax their shoulders and keep the neck in a neutral position.
If a patient has suspected cervical spine trauma or instability, do not perform routine neck movements.
Inspect the neck from the front, sides, and, where appropriate, behind.
Look for:
Symmetry of both sides of the neck.
Generalised or localised swelling.
Thyroid enlargement or goitre.
Enlarged lymph nodes.
Surgical scars.
Abnormal posture or deformity.
Visible masses or prominent veins.
Wasting or asymmetry of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
Interpretation:
Diffuse anterior swelling may indicate a goitre.
A localised lateral swelling may represent a lymph node, congenital cyst, salivary gland enlargement, or other neck mass.
A midline swelling that moves with swallowing may originate from the thyroid or another structure attached to the larynx or hyoid.
A pulsatile mass requires caution; do not aggressively palpate it.
Look for:
Redness or inflammation.
Ulcers, sinuses, or discharging wounds.
Scars from previous thyroid surgery or lymph node biopsy.
Bruising or skin tethering.
Dilated superficial veins.
Pigmentation or skin lesions.
Scars may provide clues to previous thyroidectomy, tracheostomy, neck dissection, or other surgery.
Observe the carotid region and jugular venous pulsation.
Carotid pulsation is usually a brisk arterial movement.
Jugular venous pulsation is a softer, often biphasic or undulating movement that changes with posture and respiration.
Do not confuse a prominent external jugular vein with a carotid arterial pulsation.

content_groups.group_title: D. Position of the head and neck

blocks.text: Look for:
Head tilt.
Torticollis.
Restricted spontaneous movement.
Abnormal posture caused by pain.
Head held forward or an extended neck due to respiratory distress.
Clinical warning: Stridor, rapidly progressive swelling, drooling, difficulty breathing, or inability to swallow secretions requires urgent assessment of the airway.

subsections.subsection_title: Palpation of the cervical lymph nodes

blocks.text: This is one of the most important components of neck examination.
Explain that you will gently feel the lymph nodes.
Position the patient with the neck slightly flexed to relax the muscles.
Use the finger pads of your index and middle fingers, with gentle circular movements.
Palpate systematically on both sides.
Avoid pinching the skin or pressing excessively deeply.
If a node is found, assess its characteristics.
Use the following sequence to ensure you do not miss any group.
Location: Midline beneath the chin, between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles.
Drainage includes the central lower lip, chin, floor of the mouth, and tip of the tongue.
Location: Beneath the body of the mandible.
Drainage includes much of the face, gums, teeth, anterior tongue (excluding the tip's principal submental drainage), and oral cavity.
Location: In front of the ear, behind the ear, and at the base of the skull, respectively.
Consider scalp, external ear, eyelid, and local skin infections depending on the group involved.
Location: Along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid and in the anterior cervical chain.
May enlarge in infections of the pharynx, tonsils, oral cavity, or other head and neck structures.
Location: Along the posterior border of the SCM and in the posterior triangle, anterior to the trapezius.
Enlargement may occur in viral illnesses and other infections, but persistent enlargement may require investigation.
Location: Deep to the sternocleidomastoid, following the internal jugular vein.
Includes the jugulodigastric node, associated with tonsillar drainage, and the jugulo-omohyoid node, associated with tongue drainage.
Location: In the supraclavicular fossae, immediately above the clavicles.
Particularly important because persistent enlargement can be associated with thoracic or abdominal malignancy, lymphoma, infection, or other disease.
The deep cervical nodes may be difficult to palpate individually. Examine gently and avoid excessive pressure over the carotid sheath.

content_groups.group_title: C. Characteristics of an enlarged lymph node

blocks.text: Whenever you find a node, assess the following:

rows: Exact lymph node group and side
Measure in centimetres, including the largest dimension
Mobile or fixed to underlying structures
Whether adjacent nodes feel attached to one another
Warmth, redness, ulceration, or attachment to the skin
Suggests fluid or pus in an appropriate clinical context

blocks.text: Tender, soft nodes: Often associated with acute infection or inflammation.
Rubbery nodes: May occur in lymphoma, although this is not diagnostic.
Hard or fixed nodes: Raise concern for metastatic malignancy, especially when persistent.
Matted nodes: May occur in tuberculosis, other infections, and malignancy.
Fluctuant nodes: May indicate suppuration.
Supraclavicular nodes: Deserve particular attention and often warrant prompt clinical investigation.
These are clinical clues, not definitive diagnostic rules. The patient's age, duration of swelling, associated symptoms, and examination elsewhere determine the next steps.

content_groups.group_title: D. What should you do if you find enlarged cervical nodes?

blocks.text: Examine likely drainage areas and look for a cause:
Scalp and skin.
Ears.
Nose and sinuses.
Oral cavity, teeth, and gums.
Tongue, tonsils, and pharynx.
Thyroid and other neck structures.
Other lymph node groups, liver, and spleen when indicated.
Ask about fever, sore throat, dental pain, recent infection, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, and persistent fever.

Persistent, progressive, hard, fixed, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy needs appropriate investigation. Depending on the clinical picture, this may include blood tests, ultrasound, cross-sectional imaging, or tissue sampling.
The thyroid is a major focus of neck examination.
Inspect the anterior neck for a swelling in the lower part of the neck, usually below the thyroid cartilage.
Look for:
Diffuse or nodular enlargement.
Symmetry of the thyroid lobes.
Visible nodules.
Scars from previous surgery.
Prominent veins.
Skin changes.
Movement of the swelling during swallowing.
Ask the patient to take a sip of water and swallow while observing the swelling.
Key finding: The thyroid gland typically moves upwards with swallowing because it is attached to the larynx and trachea through the pretracheal fascia.
A thyroglossal duct cyst may also move with swallowing, but characteristically moves upwards when the patient protrudes the tongue.
A common OSCE technique is palpation from behind the patient.
Stand behind the patient.
Ask them to relax their neck and slightly flex the head.
Identify the thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage, and trachea.
Locate the isthmus, which usually lies over the second to fourth tracheal rings.
Palpate the isthmus gently.
Ask the patient to swallow and feel the gland rise beneath your fingers.
Palpate each lobe in turn, using gentle pressure and, if helpful, slight displacement of the trachea.
Assess the gland for enlargement, nodules, tenderness, and consistency.
An anterior approach is also acceptable, depending on the examiner's preferred technique.

rows: Simple goitre, Graves disease, or thyroiditis, depending on other findings
Benign or malignant thyroid nodule; requires appropriate evaluation
May occur in subacute thyroiditis or other inflammatory conditions
May occur in autoimmune disease, fibrosis, or malignancy
Fixed mass or associated abnormal lymph nodes
Raises concern for invasive disease or malignancy
May cause compressive symptoms or signs of thoracic inlet obstruction

blocks.text: Palpation alone cannot reliably distinguish benign from malignant thyroid nodules.

content_groups.group_title: D. Assess the thyroid's surface and consistency

blocks.text: Determine whether the gland is:
Smooth or irregular.
Soft, firm, or hard.
Tender or non-tender.
Nodular or uniformly enlarged.
Mobile or apparently fixed.
Also assess whether enlargement is symmetrical or predominantly affects one lobe.
Ask the patient to swallow water while keeping your fingers gently over the gland.
Normal thyroid tissue usually rises with swallowing.
A thyroid swelling often rises with swallowing.
A mass that does not move as expected may arise from another structure or be tethered to surrounding tissues.
This sign is helpful but not absolute.
Use the diaphragm of the stethoscope over an enlarged thyroid, particularly when Graves disease or marked hypervascularity is suspected.
Listen for a thyroid bruit, which is a vascular sound caused by increased blood flow.
A bruit can occur in Graves disease, but its absence does not exclude the diagnosis. Do not auscultate routinely over every normal thyroid.
This is useful when a large goitre or retrosternal extension is suspected.
Ask the patient to raise both arms above the head.
Observe for facial congestion, facial cyanosis, neck vein distension, or respiratory discomfort.
Stop immediately if the patient develops significant symptoms.
A positive Pemberton's sign suggests thoracic inlet obstruction, which may be associated with a large retrosternal goitre or another compressive lesion.
It should be performed only when clinically appropriate and with caution in symptomatic patients.
A neck examination should not end after palpating the thyroid. Look for signs of altered thyroid hormone function.
Look for:
Fine tremor of the outstretched hands.
Warm, moist skin.
Tachycardia or an irregular pulse.
Lid retraction or lid lag.
Proptosis, especially in Graves disease.
Proximal muscle weakness.
Weight loss despite increased appetite.
Increased reflexes.
A thyroid bruit may also be present.
Look for:
Dry, coarse skin.
Coarse hair or hair loss.
Puffy face.
Bradycardia.
Delayed relaxation of tendon reflexes.
Slow speech or hoarse voice.
Cold intolerance and weight gain.
Constipation.
These findings may be subtle and require biochemical confirmation.
Pulse rate and rhythm.
Blood pressure.
Fine tremor assessment.
Proximal muscle power.
Deep tendon reflexes.
Eye examination for thyroid eye disease.
Thyroid function tests, usually TSH and free T4, with additional tests depending on the clinical context.
Tracheal position is important because displacement may indicate an underlying mass or changes in intrathoracic pressure or volume.
Position the patient sitting upright, with the head in a neutral position.
Identify the suprasternal notch.
Place the index finger gently in the notch and feel the trachea.
Compare the space between the trachea and the sternocleidomastoid muscles on both sides, if necessary.
Assess whether the trachea is central or displaced.
Avoid assessing the trachea with the neck excessively flexed or rotated because this may create a false impression of deviation.

rows: Normal finding, although not sufficient to exclude chest disease
Trachea displaced away from a lesion
Large thyroid mass, mediastinal mass, tension pneumothorax, or large pleural effusion
Lung collapse, pulmonary fibrosis, or other causes of ipsilateral volume loss

blocks.text: The direction of displacement must be interpreted with the clinical picture and chest examination.

Emergency point: Tracheal deviation in a patient with sudden respiratory distress, hypotension, or markedly reduced unilateral breath sounds raises concern for tension pneumothorax. Do not delay emergency management while trying to confirm deviation.

A downward movement of the trachea with each heartbeat may be described as a tracheal tug. It can be associated with significant aortic arch pathology, particularly an aortic aneurysm, but it is not a reliable standalone diagnostic sign.
The carotid arteries provide information about arterial pulsation and, in selected patients, possible vascular disease.
Inspect the neck for visible carotid pulsations.
Palpate the carotid pulse gently, one side at a time.
Assess the amplitude, character, and symmetry of the pulses.
If clinically indicated, auscultate for a bruit.
Never palpate both carotid arteries simultaneously. Bilateral compression can reduce cerebral blood flow and provoke symptoms.
Pulse volume.
Upstroke and character.
Symmetry.
Presence of an unusually forceful or diminished pulse.
Carotid bruit, if auscultation is indicated.
A carotid bruit may suggest turbulent flow but does not reliably establish the presence or severity of carotid stenosis. Significant stenosis can occur without a bruit.
Avoid vigorous carotid sinus massage as part of a routine examination. It is a specialised procedure with potential risks.

subsections.subsection_title: Examination of the jugular venous pressure (JVP)

blocks.text: JVP assessment is often included in cardiovascular examination, but it is relevant to the neck because it reflects right atrial pressure.
Position the patient at approximately 30–45 degrees.
Turn the head slightly to the left, avoiding excessive rotation.
Use tangential lighting to identify the internal jugular venous pulsation on the right side.
Adjust the bed angle until the top of the venous column can be seen.
Identify the highest point of venous pulsation.
Measure the vertical height above the sternal angle.
The conventional upper limit is approximately 3–4 cm above the sternal angle, depending on the reference and examination technique.

rows: Usually a single brisk outward impulse
Usually falls with inspiration in normal spontaneous breathing
May rise with sustained hepatojugular reflux
Does not show the same venous response

blocks.text: An elevated JVP may occur in right-sided heart failure, fluid overload, pulmonary hypertension, or pericardial disease, among other conditions.
The major salivary glands include the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands.
Inspect and palpate the area in front of and below the ear, extending towards the angle of the mandible.
Assess:
Enlargement and symmetry.
Tenderness.
Consistency and any palpable mass.
Skin changes.
Facial nerve function if a parotid mass is present.
A parotid swelling may be associated with viral parotitis, obstruction, inflammation, or a tumour.
Important: Facial nerve weakness associated with a parotid mass is a concerning feature and requires prompt specialist assessment.
Palpate beneath the body of the mandible, distinguishing glandular tissue from submandibular lymph nodes.
Assess for:
Enlargement.
Tenderness.
A palpable mass.
Possible duct obstruction or salivary calculi.
Ask about pain or swelling during meals, which may suggest salivary duct obstruction.
These are assessed mainly by inspecting and palpating the floor of the mouth when indicated. Look for swelling, duct abnormalities, or a cystic lesion such as a ranula.

subsections.subsection_title: Examination of the cervical spine and neck movements

blocks.text: This component is particularly relevant when the patient presents with neck pain, stiffness, neurological symptoms, or suspected musculoskeletal disease.
Look for:
Abnormal curvature.
Torticollis.
Muscle spasm.
Scars or swelling.
Asymmetry.
Abnormal head posture.
Palpate the cervical spinous processes and surrounding muscles gently.
Assess for:
Midline tenderness.
Paraspinal muscle tenderness.
Muscle spasm.
Deformity.
Localised swelling.
Do not perform routine range-of-motion testing if trauma or cervical spine instability is suspected.
If safe, ask the patient to perform the following movements actively:
Ask the patient to bring the chin towards the chest, then look upwards. Observe range, discomfort, and symmetry.
Ask the patient to turn the head to the left and right.
Ask the patient to bring each ear towards the corresponding shoulder without raising the shoulder.
Observe for restricted movement, pain, muscle spasm, or neurological symptoms.
If radiculopathy is suspected, a focused neurological examination of the upper limbs is required, including power, sensation, reflexes, and relevant nerve root assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: Examination of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles

blocks.text: These muscles are important for head movement and shoulder elevation.
Motor supply: Spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI), with contributions from cervical nerves for proprioception and related functions.
Function: Turns the head to the opposite side and assists with neck flexion.
Examination:
Ask the patient to turn their head to one side against your hand.
Palpate the contralateral SCM.
Repeat on the other side.
Compare strength and bulk.
Weakness or wasting may indicate spinal accessory nerve dysfunction or a local muscular disorder.
Motor supply: Spinal accessory nerve, with cervical nerve contributions.
Examination:
Ask the patient to shrug both shoulders.
Apply downward resistance.
Compare strength and symmetry.
Weakness may be associated with spinal accessory nerve injury, including after procedures in the posterior triangle of the neck.
Ask the patient to speak and listen for:
Hoarseness.
Weak or breathy voice.
Stridor.
Dysphonia.
Difficulty speaking in complete sentences.
Ask the patient to say a sustained vowel such as “aaa” if appropriate.

Hoarseness may arise from laryngeal disease, vocal cord dysfunction, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, or other causes. Persistent hoarseness associated with a thyroid mass or other neck lesion warrants further evaluation.
Airway warning: Stridor at rest or rapidly worsening voice changes associated with breathing difficulty require urgent assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: Examination of the thoracic inlet and signs of compression

blocks.text: A large thyroid or other neck mass can compress structures at the thoracic inlet.
Ask about:
Dysphagia.
Dyspnoea.
Orthopnoea.
Cough.
Hoarseness.
A sensation of neck pressure.
Difficulty lying flat.
Facial congestion when raising the arms.
Look for dilated neck veins, prominent superficial veins, respiratory distress, and evidence of tracheal deviation.
These findings may suggest compression of the trachea, oesophagus, or major veins.

subsections.subsection_title: Complete the examination with relevant regional assessment

blocks.text: A neck lump may arise from structures outside the neck itself. When indicated, examine:
Oral cavity and oropharynx: Teeth, gums, tongue, floor of mouth, tonsils, and pharynx.
Ears and scalp: Local infection or skin lesions.
Nose and sinuses: Possible sources of infection.
Chest: Lung signs or mediastinal disease.
Other lymph node groups: Axillary and inguinal nodes if generalised lymphadenopathy is suspected.
Abdomen: Liver and spleen enlargement when lymphoma or systemic disease is considered.
The extent of the examination should be guided by the presenting complaint and the findings.
Wash hands, introduce yourself, obtain consent, and position the patient.
Inspect the neck for symmetry, swelling, scars, skin changes, and visible pulsations.
Palpate submental and submandibular nodes.
Examine preauricular, postauricular, and occipital nodes.
Palpate anterior and posterior cervical chains and the supraclavicular fossae.
Assess any enlarged node for site, size, tenderness, consistency, mobility, matting, and skin changes.
Inspect the thyroid and observe its movement during swallowing.
Palpate the thyroid isthmus and both lobes; assess size, nodules, tenderness, and consistency.
Auscultate an enlarged or hypervascular thyroid when indicated.
Assess tracheal position.
Assess carotid pulses one side at a time; auscultate if indicated.
Assess JVP if performing a cardiovascular neck examination.
Examine the parotid and submandibular glands if indicated.
Assess cervical spine movements and SCM/trapezius function if relevant and safe.
Listen to the voice and look for signs of airway or compressive symptoms.
Thank the patient, help them get comfortable, wash hands, and present findings.

subsections.subsection_title: How to present your findings to an examiner

blocks.text: A normal neck examination may be reported as follows:

On examination of the neck, it is symmetrical, with no visible swelling, scars, skin changes, or dilated superficial veins. There is no palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. The thyroid gland is not enlarged, with no palpable nodules or tenderness. The trachea is central. There are no abnormal carotid pulsations or bruits, and the jugular venous pressure is not elevated. Neck movements are full and painless, with normal sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscle function. The voice is normal, with no evidence of airway compromise.
Only include findings you have actually assessed. For example, omit JVP or carotid bruit findings if you did not perform those parts of the examination.

content_groups.group_title: Example: reporting an abnormal thyroid examination

blocks.text: There is a visible, diffuse anterior neck swelling in the region of the thyroid gland. The swelling moves upwards on swallowing. On palpation, the thyroid is diffusely enlarged, smooth, non-tender, and without discrete palpable nodules. The trachea is central, and there is no palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Further assessment of thyroid function and appropriate investigations are indicated.

There is a palpable left cervical lymph node measuring approximately 2 cm in its largest dimension. It is firm, non-tender, and relatively immobile, with no overlying skin ulceration. The remaining cervical and supraclavicular lymph node groups should be assessed and documented. Given the clinical characteristics, further evaluation is warranted.
1. Why does a thyroid swelling move on swallowing?
Because the thyroid is attached to the larynx and trachea through the pretracheal fascia and moves with the larynx during swallowing.
2. What is the significance of a hard, fixed cervical lymph node?
It raises suspicion of malignancy, including metastatic disease, although other causes are possible. Further investigation is required.
3. What is the significance of a left supraclavicular lymph node?

An enlarged left supraclavicular node, classically called Virchow's node, may reflect malignancy in the thorax or abdomen, including the stomach. It may also occur in lymphoma, infection, and other conditions.
4. What causes tracheal deviation?

A mass effect may push the trachea away, while loss of lung volume may pull it towards the affected side. Large pleural effusions and tension pneumothorax are important causes of displacement away from the affected side.
5. What is a thyroid bruit?
A vascular sound heard over the thyroid due to increased blood flow, classically associated with Graves disease.
6. What is Pemberton's sign?
Development of facial congestion, cyanosis, venous distension, or respiratory symptoms when both arms are raised, suggesting thoracic inlet obstruction.
7. What are the main causes of a neck swelling?
A useful framework is:
Congenital: thyroglossal duct cyst, branchial cleft cyst, cystic hygroma.
Inflammatory or infective: lymphadenitis, abscess, salivary gland inflammation.
Thyroid: goitre, thyroiditis, benign nodules, malignancy.
Neoplastic: lymphoma, metastatic lymph nodes, salivary gland tumours.
Vascular: carotid aneurysm or other vascular lesions.
8. What should you never forget when examining a neck lump?

Assess the airway, identify the anatomical site, establish duration and progression, examine the thyroid and lymph nodes, and look for suspicious features such as fixation, progressive enlargement, persistent hoarseness, dysphagia, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Remember “I L T T C J S M V” for the major components of a comprehensive neck examination:

The precise order can vary according to the clinical presentation and OSCE station. In every case, prioritise patient safety, a systematic approach, accurate documentation, and clear interpretation of the findings.
